This article belongs to a series on geometric complexity theory (GCT), an approach to the P vs. NP and related problems through algebraic geometry and representation theory. The basic principle behind this approach is called the flip. In essence, it reduces the negative hypothesis in complexity theory (the lower bound problems), such as the P vs. NP problem in characteristic zero, to the positive hypothesis in complexity theory (the upper bound problems): specifically, to showing that the problems of deciding nonvanishing of the fundamental structural constants in representation theory and algebraic geometry, such as the well known plethysm constants--or rather certain relaxed forms of these decision probelms--belong to the complexity class P. In this article, we suggest a plan for implementing the flip, i.e., for showing that these relaxed decision problems belong to P. This is based on the reduction of the preceding complexity-theoretic positive hypotheses to mathematical positivity hypotheses: specifically, to showing that there exist positive formulae--i.e. formulae with nonnegative coefficients--for the structural constants under consideration and certain functions associated with them. These turn out be intimately related to the similar positivity properties of the Kazhdan-Lusztig polynomials and the multiplicative structural constants of the canonical (global crystal) bases in the theory of Drinfeld-Jimbo quantum groups. The known proofs of these positivity properties depend on the Riemann hypothesis over finite fields and the related results. Thus the reduction here, in conjunction with the flip, in essence, says that the validity of the P vs. NP conjecture in characteristic zero is intimately linked to the Riemann hypothesis over finite fields and related problems.

The basic principle underlying this approach is known as the flip. In essence, it reduces negative hypotheses in complexity theory—namely, lower-bound problems, such as the P vs. NP problem in characteristic zero—to positive hypotheses in complexity theory, that is, upper-bound problems. This article is part of a series devoted to geometric complexity theory (GCT), a program that uses algebraic geometry and representation theory to study the P versus NP question and related complexity problems. The central idea of this program is known as the “flip.” Broadly speaking, the flip transforms negative assertions in complexity theory—namely lower-bound questions, including the characteristic-zero version of P vs. NP—into positive assertions, or upper-bound questions. More precisely, it seeks to prove that deciding whether certain fundamental structural constants from representation theory and algebraic geometry are nonzero—such as the familiar plethysm constants, or more accurately, suitable relaxed versions of these decision problems—lies in the complexity class P.

In this article, we outline a strategy for carrying out the flip by proving that these relaxed nonvanishing decision problems are solvable in polynomial time. The proposed strategy reduces those positive complexity-theoretic claims to positivity statements in mathematics. In particular, it requires proving the existence of positive formulas—that is, formulas whose coefficients are all nonnegative—for the structural constants in question, as well as for certain related functions.

These positivity phenomena are closely connected with analogous positivity results for Kazhdan–Lusztig polynomials and for the multiplicative structural constants of canonical, or global crystal, bases in the theory of Drinfeld–Jimbo quantum groups. Existing proofs of those positivity results rely on the Riemann hypothesis over finite fields and associated theorems. Consequently, when combined with the flip, the reduction proposed here suggests that the truth of the P vs. NP conjecture in characteristic zero is deeply connected with the Riemann hypothesis over finite fields and related questions.

The article belongs to a broader series on **geometric complexity theory** (GCT), a program that applies tools from algebraic geometry, representation theory, and computational complexity to major lower bound problems such as **P vs. NP** and related separation questions. Rather than attacking these problems purely through traditional combinatorial or machine-based arguments, GCT studies the symmetries and algebraic structures underlying computational problems. In particular, it translates complexity-theoretic questions into questions about group representations, orbit closures, and structural constants arising in algebraic geometry and representation theory.

A central idea in the article is the principle known as **the flip**. In ordinary complexity theory, proving lower bounds—showing that certain problems cannot be solved efficiently—is notoriously difficult. The flip proposes a way to transform these lower bound problems into upper bound problems. More specifically, it seeks to reduce the task of proving complexity separations to the task of designing efficient algorithms for certain decision problems. These decision problems concern whether particular structural constants, such as representation-theoretic multiplicities, are zero or nonzero. Thus, instead of directly proving that one computational model cannot simulate another efficiently, the GCT program aims to show that certain algebraic obstructions can be found or verified efficiently.

The article outlines a plan for implementing this flip. The strategy is to study relaxed versions of decision problems associated with structural constants, including important examples such as **plethysm constants**. These constants measure how representations decompose under operations such as composition of Schur functors, and they play a key role in the representation-theoretic framework of GCT. The goal is to prove that the relevant relaxed decision problems lie in the complexity class **P**, meaning that they can be solved in polynomial time. If successful, this would provide the algorithmic component needed for the flip: difficult lower bound statements would be transformed into tractable upper bound statements about algebraic and representation-theoretic data.

However, the proposed reduction relies on deep mathematical positivity hypotheses. In particular, the article emphasizes the need for **positive formulae** for the relevant structural constants and associated functions. A positive formula is one in which the constant is expressed using only nonnegative coefficients, often as the number of integer points in some explicitly described polytope or through another manifestly nonnegative combinatorial rule. Such formulae are crucial because they make it possible to design efficient algorithms for deciding positivity or nonvanishing. Without positivity, cancellations between positive and negative terms can make computation and decision problems much harder. Therefore, proving these positivity hypotheses is presented as a central mathematical challenge for the GCT approach.

Finally, the article argues that the **P vs. NP conjecture in characteristic zero** is deeply connected to major positivity phenomena in mathematics, including the **Riemann hypothesis over finite fields**. The suggested connection is that certain positivity results needed for the GCT program may ultimately depend on, or be analogous to, the positivity consequences of the Weil conjectures and related results in algebraic geometry. In this view, separating complexity classes is not merely a question about algorithms or machines, but is tied to profound structural properties of algebraic varieties, representation theory, and arithmetic geometry. The article therefore presents GCT as an ambitious program linking computational complexity with some of the deepest themes in modern mathematics.

counterfactuals.output:
This article surveys a central idea in geometric complexity theory (GCT): the “flip” from proving lower bounds by obstruction to proving them through explicit construction. In the GCT program, complexity class separations such as \( \mathrm{P} \neq \mathrm{NP} \) are approached by comparing orbit closures associated with determinant and permanent polynomials. The desired lower bounds are reformulated as the existence of representation-theoretic obstructions, governed by multiplicities such as plethysm constants and generalized Littlewood–Richardson coefficients.

A key difficulty is that these multiplicities are themselves hard to understand. The flip proposes replacing nonconstructive existence questions by efficient algorithms for deciding positivity: given the relevant representation-theoretic data, determine whether the corresponding multiplicity is nonzero, preferably in polynomial time. This leads to positivity hypotheses asserting that plethysm constants admit positive, polyhedral, or combinatorial descriptions analogous to those known for Littlewood–Richardson coefficients. Such descriptions would make the search for obstructions algorithmically feasible and would turn lower-bound questions into constructive problems in algebraic geometry, representation theory, and optimization.

The article also explains why the GCT positivity program is linked to deep arithmetic geometry. In particular, the search for positive formulae for plethysm constants is compared with the role of positivity in the Weil conjectures, especially the Riemann hypothesis over finite fields. Just as Deligne’s proof establishes positivity and cancellation properties for point counts via eigenvalues of Frobenius, GCT suggests that hidden geometric structures may underlie plethysm and related multiplicities. Understanding these structures could provide the canonical bases, saturation phenomena, and decision procedures required by the flip.

By placing the flip, plethysm positivity, and the finite-field Riemann hypothesis in a common conceptual framework, the article presents GCT as a program in which complexity lower bounds are tied to the discovery of new positivity theorems in geometry and representation theory.

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize the main idea of a GCT paper that reduces P vs. NP lower bounds in characteristic zero to proving polynomial-time decidability of relaxed nonvanishing problems in representation theory.
counterfactuals.output:
The paper’s main idea is the **“flip”** in Geometric Complexity Theory (GCT): instead of trying to prove a hard circuit lower bound directly, translate the lower bound into a problem about **which irreducible representations occur in certain algebraic varieties**, and then reduce the needed lower bound to efficient decision procedures for those representation-theoretic occurrence questions.

In characteristic zero, the P vs. NP problem is modeled algebraically as separating the **permanent** from the **determinant**: show that the permanent polynomial cannot be obtained from the determinant by polynomial-size linear projections. GCT turns this into a question about orbit closures under general linear group actions:

- the determinant has an orbit closure,
- the permanent has an orbit closure,
- if the permanent orbit closure is not contained in the determinant orbit closure, then one gets the desired lower bound.

To prove noncontainment, GCT looks for **representation-theoretic obstructions**: labels of irreducible representations that occur in the coordinate ring of the permanent variety but do **not** occur in the coordinate ring of the determinant variety. Such a label acts like a certificate separating the two orbit closures.

The crucial reduction is then:

> Proving the relevant P vs. NP lower bounds in characteristic zero can be reduced to proving that certain relaxed representation-theoretic nonvanishing problems are decidable in polynomial time.

Here “nonvanishing” means deciding whether certain multiplicities are positive: for example, whether a representation occurs with nonzero multiplicity in a tensor product, symmetric power, plethysm, or orbit-coordinate ring. These multiplicities are governed by objects such as generalized Littlewood–Richardson coefficients, Kronecker coefficients, and plethysm coefficients.

The word **“relaxed”** is important. Instead of asking whether a coefficient is nonzero exactly, one asks whether it becomes nonzero after scaling the parameters, or whether an associated stretching function is nonzero. This is analogous to the saturation phenomenon for Littlewood–Richardson coefficients, where positivity after scaling can often be characterized by membership in a polytope. The hope is that the relaxed version has a polynomial-time algorithm because it is governed by convex/geometric structure.

So the strategy is:

1. Reformulate algebraic P vs. NP as a containment problem between orbit closures.
2. Reduce orbit-closure separation to finding representation-theoretic obstructions.
3. Reduce the construction/search for such obstructions to deciding nonvanishing of certain multiplicities.
4. Show that if the relevant relaxed nonvanishing problems are in polynomial time, then one can efficiently construct the obstructions needed for the lower bound.

In short, the paper proposes that the path to P vs. NP in characteristic zero may go through **efficient algorithms for positivity/nonvanishing in representation theory**. The complexity-theoretic lower bound is converted into an algorithmic and structural problem about representation multiplicities.

counterfactuals.prompt: Explain how geometric complexity theory links the P vs. NP conjecture, plethysm constants, canonical bases of quantum groups, Kazhdan-Lusztig positivity, and the Riemann hypothesis over finite fields.
counterfactuals.output:
Geometric Complexity Theory (GCT) is a program, initiated mainly by Mulmuley and Sohoni, that tries to attack major complexity separations such as

\[
\mathrm{P} \neq \mathrm{NP}
\]

or more precisely algebraic analogues such as

\[
\mathrm{VP} \neq \mathrm{VNP},
\]

by translating them into questions in algebraic geometry and representation theory. The links among plethysm constants, canonical bases, Kazhdan–Lusztig positivity, and the Riemann hypothesis over finite fields arise because GCT seeks **explicit representation-theoretic obstructions** to efficient computation, and proving that such obstructions exist seems to require deep positivity phenomena.

Below is the conceptual chain.

---

## 1. From P vs. NP to orbit closures

Instead of Boolean P vs. NP directly, GCT studies algebraic complexity classes. The central comparison is between the determinant and permanent.

- The determinant \(\det_n\) is efficiently computable, analogous to a problem in P.
- The permanent \(\operatorname{perm}_m\) is VNP-complete, analogous to NP-complete problems.

Valiant’s conjecture says roughly that the permanent cannot be expressed as a polynomial-size determinant. This is an algebraic analogue of \(\mathrm{P} \neq \mathrm{NP}\).

GCT reformulates this as a problem about group actions.

One considers the action of a general linear group \(G = GL_N\) on a space of homogeneous polynomials. The determinant and permanent define points in this space. If the permanent could be represented efficiently as a determinant, then a padded version of the permanent would lie inside the orbit closure of the determinant:

\[
\operatorname{perm}_m \in \overline{G \cdot \det_n}.
\]

Thus, to prove lower bounds, one wants to show

\[
\operatorname{perm}_m \notin \overline{G \cdot \det_n}.
\]

So the complexity problem becomes an algebraic-geometric problem: separate two orbit closures.

---

## 2. Representation-theoretic obstructions

The coordinate ring of an orbit closure decomposes into irreducible representations of \(G\). Schematically,

\[
\mathbb{C}[\overline{G \cdot f}]
= \bigoplus_{\lambda} V_\lambda^{\oplus m_\lambda(f)},
\]

where \(V_\lambda\) is an irreducible representation indexed by a partition or highest weight \(\lambda\), and \(m_\lambda(f)\) is its multiplicity.

If

\[
\overline{G \cdot \operatorname{perm}_m}
\subseteq
\overline{G \cdot \det_n},
\]

then every representation occurring in the coordinate ring of the permanent orbit closure must also occur in the determinant orbit closure, with compatible multiplicities.

Therefore, a way to prove separation is to find a highest weight \(\lambda\) such that

\[
m_\lambda(\operatorname{perm}) > m_\lambda(\det)
\]

or ideally

\[
m_\lambda(\operatorname{perm}) > 0
\quad\text{but}\quad
m_\lambda(\det)=0.
\]

Such a \(\lambda\) is called a **representation-theoretic obstruction**.

This is the first key bridge:

\[
\text{complexity lower bounds}
\quad\longrightarrow\quad
\text{multiplicities of representations}.
\]

---

## 3. Plethysm constants and Kronecker-type multiplicities

The multiplicities that appear in these coordinate rings are not arbitrary. They are governed by classical constants in representation theory, especially:

- **plethysm constants**, describing decompositions of compositions of Schur functors,
- **Kronecker coefficients**, describing tensor product multiplicities for symmetric group representations,
- related branching and invariant-theoretic multiplicities.

For example, plethysm asks how a representation such as

\[
S^\lambda(S^\mu V)
\]

decomposes into irreducibles:

\[
S^\lambda(S^\mu V)
=
\bigoplus_\nu V_\nu^{\oplus p_{\lambda,\mu}^\nu}.
\]

The integers \(p_{\lambda,\mu}^\nu\) are plethysm constants.

In GCT, deciding whether certain representations occur in determinant/permanent orbit closures requires understanding whether such constants are zero or positive, and how large they are.

So GCT links P vs. NP to questions like:

\[
p_{\lambda,\mu}^\nu > 0?
\]

or

\[
g_{\lambda,\mu,\nu} > 0?
\]

where \(g_{\lambda,\mu,\nu}\) is a Kronecker coefficient.

Thus:

\[
\mathrm{P} \neq \mathrm{NP}
\quad\leadsto\quad
\text{positivity/nonvanishing of plethysm and Kronecker constants}.
\]

---

## 4. The positivity problem

A major difficulty is that plethysm and Kronecker coefficients are notoriously hard to compute. Unlike Littlewood–Richardson coefficients, which have a positive combinatorial rule via tableaux, plethysm and Kronecker coefficients do not have comparably satisfactory positive formulas in general.

For Littlewood–Richardson coefficients, one has:

\[
c_{\lambda,\mu}^{\nu}
=
\#\{\text{certain tableaux}\},
\]

which immediately gives a positivity criterion and efficient certificates.

GCT hopes for analogous positive formulas for plethysm and Kronecker coefficients:

\[
p_{\lambda,\mu}^{\nu}
=
\#\{\text{some explicitly described combinatorial objects}\}.
\]

Such formulas would support the construction of explicit obstructions.

This is the second key bridge:

\[
\text{complexity lower bounds}
\quad\leadsto\quad
\text{positive combinatorial formulas for representation multiplicities}.
\]

---

## 5. Canonical bases of quantum groups

Where might such positive formulas come from? One major source is the theory of **canonical bases** and **crystal bases** for quantum groups, developed by Lusztig and Kashiwara.

Quantum groups \(U_q(\mathfrak{g})\) are deformations of universal enveloping algebras. Their representations often possess special bases, called canonical or global crystal bases, with remarkable positivity properties.

For example, many structure constants in canonical bases lie in

\[
\mathbb{N}[q,q^{-1}],
\]

or have nonnegative coefficients after suitable normalization.

Canonical bases have been used to give positive interpretations of several representation-theoretic multiplicities, including Littlewood–Richardson coefficients and related branching coefficients.

GCT proposes that one may need generalized canonical bases for more complicated representation-theoretic objects, such as those controlling plethysm and Kronecker coefficients.

The hope is:

\[
\text{canonical basis positivity}
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
\text{positive formula for plethysm/Kronecker constants}
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
\text{constructible obstructions}
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
\mathrm{P}\neq\mathrm{NP}.
\]

This is not a completed theorem; it is a major guiding philosophy of the GCT program.

---

## 6. Kazhdan–Lusztig positivity

Kazhdan–Lusztig theory provides another deep source of positivity.

Kazhdan–Lusztig polynomials \(P_{x,w}(q)\) arise in the representation theory of Lie algebras, Hecke algebras, Schubert varieties, and intersection cohomology. Their coefficients are nonnegative:

\[
P_{x,w}(q) \in \mathbb{N}[q].
\]

This positivity was originally conjectural and later proven using geometry: the coefficients are dimensions of intersection cohomology groups of Schubert varieties.

Canonical bases and Kazhdan–Lusztig theory are closely related. In many settings, canonical basis elements are controlled by Kazhdan–Lusztig polynomials, and their positivity comes from the same geometric mechanism: intersection cohomology and purity.

GCT draws inspiration from this. It asks whether the multiplicities relevant to complexity theory can be understood through similar geometric objects whose intersection cohomology yields nonnegative coefficients.

Thus:

\[
\text{Kazhdan–Lusztig positivity}
\quad\leadsto\quad
\text{canonical bases and positive multiplicity formulas}
\quad\leadsto\quad
\text{GCT obstructions}.
\]

---

## 7. The Riemann hypothesis over finite fields

The link to the Riemann hypothesis over finite fields comes through the proof of positivity in algebraic geometry.

The Weil conjectures, including the analogue of the Riemann hypothesis for varieties over finite fields, were proved by Deligne. They imply strong purity and positivity results for étale cohomology.

In the geometric proof of Kazhdan–Lusztig positivity, one uses intersection cohomology of varieties over finite fields. Deligne’s theory of weights, based on the Weil conjectures and the Riemann hypothesis over finite fields, implies that the relevant cohomological traces have the required positivity and purity properties.

Very roughly:

\[
\text{Riemann hypothesis over finite fields}
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
\text{purity of intersection cohomology}
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
\text{Kazhdan–Lusztig positivity}
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
\text{canonical basis positivity}.
\]

GCT hopes to exploit analogous positivity mechanisms for the harder multiplicities appearing in plethysm and Kronecker theory.

So the connection is not that the classical Riemann hypothesis directly implies \(\mathrm{P}\neq\mathrm{NP}\). Rather, the finite-field Riemann hypothesis is part of the geometric machinery that historically produced deep positivity theorems, and GCT seeks comparable positivity theorems for representation-theoretic constants relevant to complexity.

---

## 8. The full conceptual pipeline

The hoped-for GCT pipeline can be summarized as:

\[
\mathrm{P} \neq \mathrm{NP}
\]

is approached via

\[
\text{permanent not in determinant orbit closure}
\]

which is reduced to finding

\[
\text{representation-theoretic obstructions}
\]

whose existence depends on understanding

\[
\text{plethysm, Kronecker, and related multiplicities}.
\]

To understand those multiplicities, one seeks

\[
\text{positive combinatorial formulas}.
\]

Such positivity may come from

\[
\text{canonical bases of quantum groups}
\]

and related structures, whose positivity is modeled on

\[
\text{Kazhdan–Lusztig positivity}.
\]

Kazhdan–Lusztig positivity itself is deeply connected to

\[
\text{intersection cohomology, purity, and the Riemann hypothesis over finite fields}.
\]

In compressed form:

\[
\boxed{
\mathrm{P}\neq\mathrm{NP}
\;\leadsto\;
\text{orbit-closure separation}
\;\leadsto\;
\text{representation obstructions}
\;\leadsto\;
\text{plethysm/Kronecker positivity}
\;\leadsto\;
\text{canonical bases}
\;\leadsto\;
\text{Kazhdan--Lusztig positivity}
\;\leadsto\;
\text{Weil/Deligne finite-field RH}
}
\]

---

## Important caveat

This is a research program, not a completed proof.

Several early hopes of GCT, especially the possibility of “occurrence obstructions” alone separating permanent from determinant in the most direct way, have encountered serious barriers. Results by Bürgisser, Ikenmeyer, Panova and others showed limitations of certain proposed obstruction strategies.

Nevertheless, the broader GCT philosophy remains influential: it connects computational complexity to deep structures in algebraic geometry, representation theory, quantum groups, and positivity phenomena.

counterfactuals.output:
The paper argues that the central obstruction to carrying out the Geometric Complexity Theory (GCT) program for separating complexity classes such as \(P\) and \(NP\) is not merely the construction of representation-theoretic obstructions, but the development of effective positivity theorems for the structural constants governing relevant representation categories. Its thesis is that a sufficiently strong theory of positivity—analogous to the Littlewood–Richardson positivity theory in type \(A\)—would make the GCT “flip” feasible: instead of proving lower bounds directly by exhibiting hard functions, one would prove the existence of efficiently verifiable representation-theoretic certificates separating orbit closures attached to easy and hard computational problems.

In GCT, complexity-class separation is reformulated geometrically. One associates to a computational problem, such as the permanent or determinant, an algebraic variety or orbit closure under a reductive group action. The question whether one problem efficiently reduces to another becomes a question about containment of orbit closures or their coordinate rings. To prove non-containment, one seeks an irreducible representation occurring in the coordinate ring of one variety but not in the other. Such a representation is called an obstruction. Thus, the lower-bound problem is transformed into a problem about comparing multiplicities of irreducible representations.

The relevant multiplicities are structural constants of representation theory: Littlewood–Richardson coefficients, Kronecker coefficients, plethysm coefficients, and more general constants arising in coordinate rings of orbit closures and invariant-theoretic quotients. In principle, an obstruction exists if there is a highest weight \(\lambda\) such that the associated representation occurs with positive multiplicity on the “hard” side but with zero or smaller multiplicity on the “easy” side. Therefore, the feasibility of the GCT program depends on being able to decide positivity and nonvanishing of these multiplicities efficiently.

The paper emphasizes that for classical Littlewood–Richardson coefficients, positivity is governed by a remarkably tractable polyhedral/combinatorial theory. The saturation theorem of Knutson and Tao states that a Littlewood–Richardson coefficient \(c_{\lambda,\mu}^{\nu}\) is positive if and only if its stretched version \(c_{k\lambda,k\mu}^{k\nu}\) is positive for some—or equivalently every sufficiently appropriate—positive integer \(k\). Moreover, positivity can be characterized by the existence of integral points in explicitly described polytopes, such as hive polytopes. This yields short certificates for nonvanishing and places the decision problem in polynomial time. The paper takes this paradigm as the model for what is needed in GCT.

However, the constants naturally arising in GCT are much harder than Littlewood–Richardson coefficients. Kronecker coefficients, which describe tensor products of irreducible representations of symmetric groups or, equivalently, certain \(GL\)-representation decompositions, lack a comparably simple positive rule. Plethysm coefficients, which govern decompositions such as \(S^{d}(S^{e}V)\) into irreducibles, are even more elusive. Yet these coefficients appear precisely in the comparison of coordinate rings relevant to determinant-versus-permanent and related complete problems. Thus, the paper identifies the absence of positivity formulae for Kronecker and plethysm-type constants as a principal mathematical bottleneck in GCT.

The proposed route is to establish positivity hypotheses for these structural constants. Roughly, such hypotheses assert that nonvanishing of a coefficient is equivalent to the feasibility of an associated system of linear inequalities, or to the existence of an integral point in a polytope or more general convex-geometric object, with polynomially bounded descriptions. Stronger versions include saturation-type statements: positivity of a stretched coefficient should stabilize in a controlled way, so that deciding positivity reduces to rational feasibility. Even if exact saturation fails, a weaker “approximate saturation” or “quasi-polynomial saturation” may suffice, provided the obstruction search remains algorithmically efficient.

This positivity theory is not presented as a peripheral combinatorial desideratum, but as the mechanism that could make lower bounds provable. GCT seeks “explicit obstructions”: representation labels \(\lambda\) whose validity can be checked in time polynomial in the input size. If positivity of the relevant structural constants has short certificates, then the existence of obstructions can be searched for, verified, and potentially constructed using algorithms from linear programming, integer programming in controlled dimension, or polyhedral combinatorics. Positivity would therefore turn the intractable lower-bound problem into a structured, finite, and algorithmically accessible problem in representation theory.

The paper further argues that this constitutes a “flip” in the sense of replacing a hard nonexistence statement—no small circuit computes a given function—by the existence of a polynomially verifiable certificate. Instead of attempting to prove directly that every polynomial-size circuit fails, one proves that a certain representation occurs on one side of an orbit-closure comparison and not on the other. The burden then shifts to showing that the relevant multiplicity inequalities can be certified through positive combinatorial models. Positivity is thus the analogue, within algebraic complexity theory, of the certificate structure that makes many problems amenable to algorithmic proof.

A key philosophical point is that the positivity required for GCT is expected to be deeper than known total-positivity or canonical-basis phenomena but possibly related to them. The paper situates the desired hypotheses among major results in geometric representation theory: standard monomial theory, canonical bases, moment polytopes, geometric invariant theory, and the theory of quantum groups. These frameworks often explain why structural constants are nonnegative and sometimes provide combinatorial parametrizations. GCT requires analogous constructions for the plethystic and Kronecker regimes, where existing tools are incomplete.

The paper also stresses that mere numerical algorithms for computing coefficients are insufficient. Exact computation of Kronecker or plethysm coefficients may be computationally hard, and even when possible it does not give conceptual control over the asymptotic representation semigroups needed for orbit-closure separation. What is required is a structural understanding of positivity: criteria that reveal when coefficients vanish, when they are positive, how positivity behaves under stretching, and how these phenomena interact with the representation-theoretic geometry of determinant and permanent orbit closures.

In this framework, proving positivity properties would contribute to GCT in three linked ways. First, it would make occurrence and nonoccurrence of relevant representations decidable by efficient certificates. Second, it would enable the construction of candidate obstructions through convex-geometric or combinatorial search. Third, it would provide the mathematical rigidity needed to show that obstructions exist asymptotically for all sufficiently large input sizes. The separation \(P \ne NP\), or its algebraic analogue \(VP \ne VNP\), would then follow from the systematic production of such obstructions.

The paper’s argument is therefore conditional but programmatic: if one can establish robust positivity and saturation-type theorems for the structural constants governing the coordinate rings of orbit closures in GCT, then the representation-theoretic obstruction strategy may become executable. The main mathematical challenge is to extend the known positivity miracles of Littlewood–Richardson theory to the far more difficult constants arising from Kronecker products, plethysm, and invariant theory. In this sense, the route to major complexity lower bounds is presented as passing through a new, highly nontrivial positivity theory in geometric representation theory.

In summary, the paper contends that the GCT approach to \(P\) versus \(NP\) hinges on converting lower-bound questions into positivity questions for representation-theoretic structural constants. Positivity theorems would supply explicit, efficiently checkable obstructions to orbit-closure containment, thereby realizing the GCT flip. The success of the program depends on discovering saturation, polyhedral, or canonical-basis-like structures for Kronecker, plethysm, and related constants comparable in power to those known for Littlewood–Richardson coefficients.
